director.chapterArc: Jab delays the decision until arithmetic defeats avoidance, then converts terror into method: inspect the unstable spruce, give Tonk a task, prepare the crossing, and prove it twice. Tonk’s remembered bridge trauma turns the crossing from a technical problem into a test of Jab’s promise to keep carrying him. The failed lashing destroys that controlled procedure; Jab survives by collapsing onto the tree, inventories the trap, overcomes a brief physiological block, and cuts them free. The crawl to safety resolves the immediate danger but exposes the deeper loss: Tonk’s leg is worse, Jab’s power is spent, and two medicines are ruined. He hides that devastation behind an ordinary face and practical tasks. Tonk’s unnamed tree closes the chapter on a small return to childhood rather than triumph.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder grounded and measured. Jab’s fear appears through arithmetic, breath, grip, cold, and repeated checks—not vocal panic. Preserve the exact mechanics of the crossing and entrapment even at the crisis peak; urgency must not blur spatial logic. Tonk’s distress is small-bodied and raw without becoming theatrical. Treat the metal as a familiar tool, not spectacle. The medicine count is the emotional nadir: land it plainly, then let Jab’s ordinary face restore functional warmth.

cues.delivery: Let the tree’s movement tighten the voice without enlarging it; Jab reads a warning, suppresses the startle, and converts it immediately into a factual risk assessment.
cues.from: He climbed up onto the root ball, and the whole tree moved.
cues.through: So: not anchored. The root ball was sitting in the mud of its own hole and the crown was tangled in alder, and between those two facts the tree was staying where it was. It would hold a man's weight. It had just told him that it would rather not.
cues.reason: The crossing changes from merely difficult to visibly unstable.

cues.delivery: Use practical warmth beneath the blunt terms: Jab offers Tonk the dignity of being told the whole plan while quietly removing any burden of decision.
cues.from: "Right," he said. "I'm going to tell you the whole of it, and then you can say what you think, and then I'm going to do it anyway. That's how this one goes."
cues.through: "There's a tree fallen across the water up there. It's a big one. It's as wide as this rock and it's not going anywhere, and I can walk across it, and so can anybody. Here's the part you won't like. I'm going to take the bag over first, on my own, without you. Then I'm coming back. Then I'm carrying you over. That's two times over and one time back, and you'll be sitting right here in the middle of it on your own for about — " he did the count honestly " — for about as long as it takes to sing the four verses twice."
cues.reason: Jab begins managing Tonk’s fear through honesty and structure.

cues.delivery: Let Tonk’s refusals rise through shortening breath and insistence, never caricaturing a child; the final remembered accusation should arrive with startling clarity.
cues.through: "You went on it before," Tonk said, and started to cry.
cues.reason: Tonk’s resistance reveals remembered trauma rather than ordinary reluctance.

cues.delivery: Keep the bridge memory physically contained under the ribs. State the past without reenacting it, then land the discovery that Tonk remembers as the wound Jab cannot reason away.
cues.from: Jab had known it was coming and it went into him anyway, low down, under the ribs, where he did not have a guard for it.
cues.through: He remembered something, though. He remembered enough to look at a fallen tree over a creek and start crying.
cues.reason: The concealed family trauma becomes present and shared.

cues.delivery: Close the distance without sentimentality. Jab makes safety out of facts and continued responsibility; let Tonk’s literal request for Little release only a thread of pressure.
cues.from: "Come here," Jab said, and put his forehead against his brother's forehead, which was all the holding you could do to a boy strapped into a frame. "Listen. I know. I know what it looks like. I'm going to tell you two things and they're both true."
cues.through: Tonk looked down at his hand. "Oh," he said.
cues.reason: Jab answers panic with contact, logic, and the promise that he is still carrying Tonk.

cues.delivery: Hold the question gently but do not soften the truth. The unsteady hand is the admission; the promise about himself should be quiet, exact, and absolute.
cues.from: "What if you don't come," Tonk said.
cues.through: "Tonk." Jab put his hand on the side of his brother's face. His own hand was not steady and he did not bother hiding it, because the one thing he had refused to do for six weeks was lie to him about anything that mattered. "I'll come. That's not a promise about the water. That's a promise about me."
cues.reason: Jab distinguishes an honest commitment from a false guarantee of safety.

cues.delivery: Almost under the breath, address the worn lashing as if enforcing a bargain; let exhaustion show, not superstition.
cues.from: "Four days," he said to it. "You said four days."
cues.through: "Four days," he said to it. "You said four days."
cues.reason: A private line exposes how much depends on failing material.

cues.delivery: Make Jab’s instructions steady enough for Tonk to borrow. His mild humor about the water is tactical reassurance, while Tonk’s tightly shut eyes remain literal rather than cute.
cues.through: "I'm going to shut my eyes," Tonk said, and shut them, hard, with his whole face.
cues.reason: Jab regulates Tonk immediately before the dangerous crossing.

cues.delivery: Make the failure sudden, then keep every shift of weight, hand, knee, and frame surgically clear. Fear is the load continuing to turn him, not faster speech or action-film force.
cues.from: He was eight feet into the sag when the shoulder lashing let go.
cues.through: Then it stopped trying, because he had not let it, and the tree bounced twice under them and went still.
cues.reason: The controlled crossing collapses into a genuine near-fatal fall.

cues.delivery: Use clipped, low-pressure questions as an injury inventory disguised as reassurance. Tonk’s tiny answer brings relief, but Jab must keep the steadiness working rather than celebrate.
cues.through: "Good. Don't move. Don't help. I've got you and this is fine."
cues.reason: Jab re-establishes contact and control after the fall.

cues.delivery: Compress the fear into breath control and exact movement. When the metal fails, narrow and quiet the delivery; the grinding water should register as indifferent pressure, not a dramatic flourish.
cues.from: "All right," Jab said out loud. "All right."
cues.through: Under him the water went on grinding stones along the bed.
cues.reason: Jab discovers he is trapped and his essential tool will not answer.

cues.delivery: Keep Tonk small and direct. Jab’s repeated answers should acknowledge the pain without offering comfort he cannot guarantee.
cues.from: "Jab," said Tonk. "The stick's in my leg place."
cues.reason: Tonk identifies the injury while Jab remains unable to free him.

cues.delivery: Let the scream and hopeless crying land as observed physical facts. Keep Jab’s repeated six words workmanlike and close, grief expressed through holding and staying.
cues.from: Getting Tonk out took a long time because the frame would not sit straight any more and everything had to be done left-handed and wrong. When the leg came off the rail his brother screamed in a way Jab had not heard since the first three nights, and then kept crying afterward in the exhausted, hopeless way that was far worse, and Jab knelt in the wet leaves holding him and saying the same six words over and over until the crying went down to hiccups.
cues.through: Getting Tonk out took a long time because the frame would not sit straight any more and everything had to be done left-handed and wrong. When the leg came off the rail his brother screamed in a way Jab had not heard since the first three nights, and then kept crying afterward in the exhausted, hopeless way that was far worse, and Jab knelt in the wet leaves holding him and saying the same six words over and over until the crying went down to hiccups.
cues.reason: Safety exposes the renewed severity of Tonk’s pain.

cues.delivery: Approach the forbidden question with quiet self-recognition; the lack of an answer is depletion, not mystical suspense. Finish hollow and factual.
cues.from: The leg had been jarred hard and twice. The wrapping had slipped and there was fresh clear wet on it, and the whole lower leg had gone tighter and hotter than it had been that morning, and Jab put his hands either side of it without touching and held them there and, for one bad moment, asked the thing in his chest the question he had promised himself he would only ask when he did not care about the answer.
cues.through: It did not answer. He had nothing left to ask it with.
cues.reason: Jab breaks his own rule and discovers that even the unreliable resource is exhausted.

cues.delivery: Keep the ruined medicine painfully ordinary: wet paper, paste, disposal, counting. Do not mourn aloud; isolate the final number and let its practical meaning carry the loss.
cues.from: He got the wrapping right. He got Tonk propped against the pack under the biggest alder with the hide over him. Then he opened his coat for the birch paper and found the front of it soaked through where he had lain in the spray on the log, and the paper had gone soft, and when he unfolded it the outer two twists came apart on his fingers into a gray wet paste that smelled like a wet stump and was not medicine any more.
cues.reason: Two irreplaceable medicines are destroyed, deepening the crisis after apparent escape.

cues.delivery: Put the ordinary face audibly in place: brisk, believable tasks offered as shelter. Warmth is present but concealed inside competence.
cues.from: "Right," he said, and turned round with a twist in his hand and his ordinary face on. "Here's yours. And then I'm going to build you the best fire you've ever seen, and I'm going to fix this frame, and you're going to tell me what we're calling that tree."
cues.through: "Right," he said, and turned round with a twist in his hand and his ordinary face on. "Here's yours. And then I'm going to build you the best fire you've ever seen, and I'm going to fix this frame, and you're going to tell me what we're calling that tree."
cues.reason: Jab masks the medicine loss and rebuilds Tonk’s sense of safety through routine.

cues.delivery: Give Tonk’s conclusion literal seriousness with only the faintest dry lift; it is a return to naming and childhood, not a punchline.
cues.from: "That one hasn't got a name," he said.
cues.through: "That one hasn't got a name," he said.
cues.reason: The chapter ends on a restrained release from crisis into normal childish logic.
